utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. There are a couple of matters that the Chamber wishes to deal with before we continue with the evidence. First, on the 6th of February, in order to provide sufficient notice, the Chamber informed the parties via e-mail that it had decided to exclude paragraphs 3 to 35 of the proposed Rule 92 ter statement for Gojko Klickovic's statement, who is scheduled to testify today. Having reviewed the statement, the Chamber found that these paragraphs pertained exclusively to Bosanska Krupa, a municipality withdrawn from the indictment. The Chamber allowed the remainder of the statement which pertained to the witness's background and to character evidence of the accused to be presented pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Second, on the same day, the Chamber ordered that the accused's filing entitled, "Statement of General Mladic," and filed on the same day be temporarily reclassified as confidential. The Chamber will now rule on the permanent status of this filing. Having heard the parties' submissions, the Chamber is still of the view that this filing directly infringes upon a Chamber's order and serves absolutely no purpose before this Chamber. Accordingly, the Chamber instructs the Registry to expunge the filing from the filing records of this case, replace it with a certificate referring to this order by the Chamber, and place the filing in the confidential case correspondence folder. The Prosecution's motion to strike the accused's 6th of February filing, filed on 7th of February, 2014, is therefore moot. I would add, Mr. Robinson, that the Chamber has heard your reasons for submitting this filing but wants to make it very clear that it will not tolerate the public record of this case being used for anything other than the interests of justice. This filing clearly did not fit into this category. That's that. We'll bring in the next witness.

So those municipalities that have been excluded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Chamber has been very consistent on this issue, and you may consult with Mr. Robinson. Good morning, Mr. Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Rasevic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something to might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question; but, in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Rasevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: When I said "for the most part," I meant that certainly some points should -- some points would require broader explanations but I accept this statement as it is. What is written there is part of what I know and part of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the transcript says "essence." In addition to these broader explanations, is there anything else that you would like to change in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.text: Otherwise you have no objection Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF

utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4307, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, I'm go to read out in the English language a brief summary of Mr. Mitar Rasevic's statement. [In English] Mitar Rasevic was the chief of security in the KP Dom in Foca before and after the outbreak of the war. Before the war, the KP Dom was a prison for the treatment of alcoholics, drug addicts, and tuberculosis prisoners. The KP Dom was an organ of the state administration and Mitar Rasevic was in charge of the guards and their conduct. If the guards were in violation of orders or misconduct, their actions were reported and appropriate punishments given. A few days before war broke out, he noticed that a number of the prisoners were released but did not return which was carried out on the order of the warden. Further, at roughly the same time, a large number of convicts escaped. At the outbreak of war, a new warden was appointed by the Crisis Staff. The army then commanded the KP Dom from the beginning of the war. Mitar Rasevic was not invited to any meetings with military or civilian authorities, and he had no personal knowledge of paramilitary units in the KP Dom. Mitar Rasevic was aware that the prisoner capacity in the prison had been exceeded at the beginning of the war; however, bunk-beds were installed as quickly as possible to alleviate this issue. Further, when the heating broke, attempts were made to repair it and cauldrons were heated to make bathing possible and the kitchen was reorganised to allow the cooking to continue. No distinction was made between prisoners of war and convicts. Despite the food shortages, a minimum number of meals was endeavoured to be provided. The KP Dom has an arrangement with the hospital in Foca and a doctor would visit twice or three times a week. The prisoners would also be taken to the hospital if necessary and a nurse was present at the KP Dom at all times. Mitar Rasevic visited the prisoners in solitary confinement daily and spoke to them personally, ensuring that they were not being mistreated; the prisoners confirmed that they were not. If a prisoner had been in solitary confinement for an extended period, Mitar Rasevic would ask that their case be re-examined. As Mitar Rasevic was unable to attend meetings at which the running of the KP Dom was discussed, he was frequently provided with orders which he had no input to, he was ordered to transport prisoners, or prepare them to be handed over for the military police. Mitar Rasevic did not have any input into the creation of these lists; he merely read them out. Never during his employment at the KP Dom was he present or aware of any prisoners being beaten or mistreated, and no prisoners ever complained to him about being mistreated. On the infrequent occasio he saw a guard mistreating a prisoner in an interrogation, he would ask for the interrogation to be stopped and the guard's conduct was reported. Further, an order was created by the warden that prohibited interrogations after 20 -- 8.00 in the evening as the guards did not feel that investigating the prisoners in the evening was the proper thing to do. There were also no mass interrogations after July or August 1992. The lists of people to be interrogated were sent from the army and the guards in the KP Dom fulfilled their orders. Mitar Rasevic was not aware of any prisoners being killed during an interrogation. The only deaths in the KP Dom were by natural causes or suicide. Mitar Rasevic never saw or was aware of any bodies being moved from the KP Dom, and he never saw traces of blood in the square or on the walls of the KP Dom. He never noticed large numbers of prisoners going missing during the day or night. The only prisoners taken away were with the army's authorisation. When he conducted night inspections, he saw that everything was okay and that the guards were in their positions. And that is the short summary. Now I would like to pose several questions to Mr. Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, how did the KP Dom function? On which basis? Did you have any rules of your own?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the KP Dom functioned as an institution before the war, during the war, after the war, and it is certainly functioning now too, on the basis of the Law on Criminal Sanctions as established by the government. The rules on internal organisation and on the job descriptions within the KP Dom were passed by the warden of the KP Dom, and on the basis of that document, further rulings were elaborated for guards duty, for instance, because each and every post had its specific characteristics. In 1992, when the war broke out, we applied, we continued to apply this very same Law on Criminal Sanctions, and the same rules on internal organisation, just like before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would just like that ask you kindly to speak a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D09672; could that please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is that we see before us now? It is in Cyrillic. Unfortunately, the translation hasn't been completed yet.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: The rules on the internal organisation of the KP Dom Foca, August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had anything been changed in relation to the previous legal provisions that were contained in such rules?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: As far as these rules are concerned, nothing was changed. It was simply copied, and work was done on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, there is a reference to prisoners and detainees. Did anything change in terms of the organisation of life in that sense?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is only natural that the category of military prisoners of war was something new that we had to deal with once the war started. However, as far as the implementation of these rules is concerned, they were treated the same way as all other persons were treated; persons who were imprisoned, detained at the KP Dom Foca, regardless of ethnicity, regardless of the type of crime for which they had been detained.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 9 in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. It already disappeared. But for the record, what is this KP Dom an abbreviation of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] KP Dom is abbreviated for "kazneno-popravni Dom," which is a correctional penal facility. Only the noun has changed in the meantime. At that time, it was called KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So "kazneno-popravni" means "correctional facility"? Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, may I be of assistance [In English] "kazneno," punish -- punishing -- I mean in accordance with punishment; and "popravni" means correction to rehabilitate and return the convict to the society.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is regulated on this basis; and what you were out of all of this? Actually, can you read out loud what number 1 says and what number 2 says.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Number 1 is the head of the guards service. That was me at the time. That's what it was called. There is a full job description there, containing all the tasks of this head of the guard service. As for number 2, that was called the supervisor of the guards. This is a kind of komandir. There were four such persons. They were in charge of working with the guards. They were in charge of internal security, external security. So they were sort of deputies of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move on to the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just tell us, please, 3, 4, 5, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Three is guard, there's a description of that; then 4 is the head of the service for re-education; and 5 are the instructors within that service for rehabilitation, counselors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you briefly tell us what number 6 is and what number 8 is?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Again, that is within that service, that was the education of persons who were detained and cultural and educational activities. There was even a secondary school before the war. Then number 7 is the department for criminal sanctions and for keeping records for such persons, so these were the persons who were in charge of documentation; and then number 8 within this educational department, there is a person who was in charge of providing employment, work to the person who were serving their sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this employment mean? Ah, I see, yes, you already referred to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 13 in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what these services are that are referred to here?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: The KP Dom also treated alcoholics, drug addicts. It had a separate section, a medical section, if I may call it that. Before the war, a general practicer, a doctor, was employed on a full-time basis. We had a dental technician. We had two medical technicians. This is under 11, 12, and 13. And then item 14 is a special service, legal affairs service. This is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the rest refers to internal organisation and administration.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document for identification purposes before -- until a full translation is provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark for identification cover page and pages 9 to 13.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4308, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it needs to be 8. Starting at page 8. Not 9. Eight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Thank you. Yes, I referred to the e-court page 9 which is page 8 in hard copy. Yes. Pages from 9 to 13 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, I see that you had a kitchen. Meals were provided. Are you able to tell us anything about the provision of food when the war broke out. How were the inmates fed and did you have sufficient quantities of food? Were there any shortages or was food denied; and on what basis?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you right away. When I came back to KP Dom in mid-May sometime, what I found was that the KP Dom was in ruins pretty much. It was destroyed. And this destruction began at the beginning of the war, when I was still there. The worst thing about it was the boiler room which was actually the key installation, if I may put it that way. It ran on coal. It was pretty much damaged because of shelling. The coal, the burning of the coal provided the steam and that was the basis for the kitchen. That's what the kitchen ran on. The pipes were broken, and without major repairs it actually could not operate. In such a situation we had to make do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, thank you. We do not need to go into all the things already said in the statement. I'm just interested in quantities and how you obtained the necessary quantities. In the statement, you said that the number of inmates rose. How did you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Since the number of prisoners rose, we asked for help from the army. We asked them to supply us with a certain quantity of foodstuffs because they were under the control of the army. So the army was obliged to do this. We also had a farm that belonged to the KP Dom or -- and that's where we also got some of our supplies. It was difficult but we did manage to at least provide minimal quantities of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was food denied? Was there any discrimination; and, if so, on what basis? On what grounds was this done?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: No. As for the KP Dom services, I can say with full responsibility that there was no discrimination whatsoever. This wasn't even technically feasible. Food was cooked in an improvised cauldron which we received from the army, and everything was put into this cauldron. And it was not possible to separate food for different categories. And I state this with certainty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please ask -- be asked to repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D09670.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document? Can you see what it's about? And can you read to us to whom it was addressed and what it -- it is requesting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: This is it a document of the 21st of October, 1992. It's addressed to the Foca Red Cross. And it's a request for packages to be issued to captured and detained persons as far as -- within auxiliary assistance programme to prisoners and inmates. Persons located in this facility require 130 packages of assistance for the imprisoned and convicted persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this 100 or 130 packages?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4309, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness see 1D09671.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated the 5th of March, 1993. Could you please explain -- could you tell us something about it? It's addressed to the Foca military barracks. And it says, "Based on the contract on leasing KP Dom facilities for detained persons," and there are captured Muslim and Serb individuals already in the Dom. Could you please tell us more about this document. What did this mean?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: When I returned to KP Dom in mid-May, the warden said that he had signed a contract with military post in Foca, the military command there, to place captured person and all soldiers who commit any kind of violation to KP Dom in Foca, that the contract specifies that they would take care of food and also the conditions of the accommodation of those individuals. I saw that contract for the first time during my own court proceedings. It was kept by the warden. Based on this, from March 1993, probably the warden asked the military post to provide certain quantities of food in order to feed that category of persons. I also would like to add that we requested on a daily basis things. We even sold furniture around Montenegro in order to buy foodstuffs for those funds in order to provide a reasonable amount of food for everyone. This was a problem that we were struggling with. We were looking for a way. Often we did not have understanding for our problem, but we did do our utmost to provide those people, regardless of who they were, to provide optimal conditions for them while they were staying in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you allow me, I'm going to read it. This is a request for beans, 200 kilograms; rice, 200 kilograms; potatoes, 200 kilograms; cooking oil, and so on and so forth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4310, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did the army respond? Did they deliberately keep the food, meaning that they had the food but did not provide it? What is your experience on this matter, as far as the KP Dom is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not get the impression that they did not provide it deliberately. Quite the contrary. They would intervene in certain cases. The army had problems with feeding their own troops at the front. This is a problem that can get very complicated easily. It's very difficult to satisfy everybody when there is a shortage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D09669.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, the receipts stamp says that it's the 18th of September, 1993. Could you please tell us what this komanda TG Foca is and what they have to do with you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: The tactical group command in Foca, as I said, was in charge of prisoners of war and soldiers who had committed some sort of crime or misdemeanour. I said earlier that the army increasingly had problems with supplying the army at the front. This was particularly pronounced, and we also felt this at the KP Dom, once Serbia imposed sanctions. Then we were not able to sell anything or buy anything from Serbia. The deputy commander, Colonel Milan Maljkovic, from what I can see, issued an order that quantities of food for military units be reduced due to food shortages. I think this is what it's about in the briefest possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the title of the document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Reduction of the portions of food articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at 2: Those are going home to spend the night are not allowed to receive food rations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because some soldiers would eat at home and now this is something that the army banned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document as a MFI document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4311.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question and one more document during the examination-in-chief. Mr. Rasevic, did you ever have an opportunity to find out anything about preparations for war and anything about the question of establishing illegal units? Do you have any knowledge about that? And is that knowledge something that is confirmed in practice?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say this: I worked in an institution that was a multi-ethnic one, and I must say that - and I'm proud of that - I must say that there were no pronounced multi-ethnic conflicts among the officials of KP Dom, and, in particular, in my service. Tensions in Foca already began in 1992 with the well-known Focatrans affair. This is a transport company. During my own trial, I learned, based on an interview from a SDA functionary in Foca who said in this interview which was given either before or after -- during or after the war, boasted that as early as 1992, in Ustikolina, which was part of the Foca municipality, he formed an armed unit numbering 100 men, which was under the command of Cavrk who died. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand you correctly: Was this in 1992 or 1990?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1990. I'm sorry if I said 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the witness talk about his own trial in his statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that he did, Your Excellency, in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D09668, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to tell the Trial Chamber what this publication is, "Oslobodjenje"?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: This is a newspaper that was published in Sarajevo even before the war. During the war, it was also published, I don't know where. It's a newspaper where this interview appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it the leading newspaper in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was considered and still is probably an official newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, actually, since -- [Overlapping speakers] ... since quite some time now he is leading. Witness speaks of 1992 and then he says is it not that you speak of 1990. That was already when I wanted to jump up but it was too late. And now it continues like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the person who gave this interview?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: It is Halid Cengic. He was a high-ranking personality in the SDA party, in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see the following page. Can we enlarge the central part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read out what it says. It's a -- under the subheading, line 20, and it says: "But as early as the 2nd of August, 1990, he established an illegal unit at Ustikolina. The 18th," or is it 180, I can't see well, "of them swore on the Qur'an that in the name of Allah they would fight for the defence and the religion of Bosnia and the Bosniak people." Did you know that and how did this tally with your information about their organisations even before the war?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: It is possible that I misspoke when I said 1992 because, actually, the year was 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did this reflect on the relations in Foca before the war?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Even then their relations were not so good in the Foca municipality. The very fact that the establishment of two transport companies began, one where there were only Muslims, and the other where there were only Serbs - both as staff and as issuers of the services - we, at the KP Dom were able, until the beginning of the war, maintain -- to maintain good relations and to avoid any effect of all that on us, the KP Dom, because although this institution was very interesting to the ethnic parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tender this document offered for identification. It will be good if we could have it entirely translated because it speaks about the roots of the conflict in Foca?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we have a basis to admit this one through this witness. All he commented upon was a year. Please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Excellencies. But for the record, the witness said that they were aware of this and that in spite of all that, they were able to preserve good relations at the KP Dom. But if you don't want it, all right. No more questions at this point, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, until recently you served a seven-years prison term for your participation in the events in the KP Dom Foca; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And your colleague, Mr. Todovic, the assistant warden in the KP Dom, was convicted in the same trial as you to a person term of 12 years and six months; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Krnojelac, the warden of the KP Dom, was convicted in a trial before this Tribunal to a prisoner term of 15 years. You are aware of this; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me quote from the appeals judgement of the 6th of November, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Your Honours, it is 65 ter 25870, page 29 in the English and page 31 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And referring to the treatment of the non-Serb detainees in the KP Dom, the judgement states and refers to: "A gross and flagrant denial of fundamental rights of the individuals in violation of international law such as the right to life, liberty, and security, the right not to be subjected to torture or to human or degrading treatment, on the grounds of membership in a group of people or a community of a different ethnicity and religion." Mr. Rasevic, that sums up the findings of, in your trial in Bosnia, on the treatment for the non-Serb detainees in the KP Dom. And you do not deny the truth of that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I will always deny that this was done by members of the guards service. I got no information from prisoners that they had been maltreated by the professional guards of Foca KP Dom. As for the conduct of others during the interrogation, during interrogations, I had no information about it. Maybe they didn't dare report it, or they thought that I was unable to do anything about it. At any rate, I cannot comment that. But I can make comments with regard to the service I was the head of; namely, that I had no information to the effect that they were doing that in an organised and systematic manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this page please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, since it has been put to the witness, I don't see any reason why it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we do without it, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff? The Chamber has a general reservation about receiving the judgement of other chamber or the other court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I thought the reservation related to the judgements from this Tribunal but not from the other tribunals, but -- or other courts, but I have no problem. I have cited it, so I have no problem. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Rasevic, I also want to refer to a -- the appeals judgement related to page 32 and in the English, in page 34 in the B/C/S, because it states in this part of -- of the appeals judgement that your sentence of originally eight years and six months was reduced to seven years because of your attempts to alleviate the suffering of the detainees, coupled with your sincere remorse. Mr. Rasevic, do you still feel this sincere remorse of what happened to the non-Serbs in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber allows me to explain a little, to clarify. Throughout my professional career, I was a true professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, our time is very limited, so I think your answer could actually be a yes or no, and we come to more details later on anyway.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, even today, I am truly sorry for everything that happened to those people later and what I learned about that. As a human being, I will always feel remorse.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You were interviewed as a suspect by the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor in September and October 2004 here in The Hague. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I mostly do. But it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And let me just cite something that you said then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we please have 65 ter 25867 on the screen, page 249.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Rasevic, we only have it in English language so you cannot read it in your own language. But I'll read slowly: "But I will tell you one thing, I felt a great deal of compassion to the people who were imprisoned there. And it was very difficult for me to see my former teacher, my neighbours, and friends with whom I celebrated almost every new year being held there. And there was nothing I could do to help them except to sneak some items to them in secret. "I deeply and sincerely regret the fate that befell all of these people that you mentioned." And a few lines further down you say: "And I will personally apologise to these people to their faces." And then further down a little bit, it says: "And I strongly oppose all the evil that was done to these people and I condemn all of those who did that to them. And I think that these people need to be punished because that is the only way that we can put an end to this evil." Mr. Rasevic, when you speak of those people that need to be punished for the evil done to the non-Serbs in the KP Dom, were you referring to the Crisis Staff and the military command who decided about arrests, detention, and interrogations?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Don't put things that way. I think that those people really should be punished who assumed the right to do what they did. I don't know whether it was the Crisis Staff who did it. I know that those people were brought in based on a document that the military post forwarded to the KP Dom, but who the people were who gave the orders and later misused some -- somebody's order, these people should be punished. I'm not an investigator, so I cannot go into that. But I think that not only here but in any part of Bosnia-Herzegovina all people who assumed the right to take somebody's life without a trial should be held responsible, no matter whether it happened in Foca, Sarajevo, Travnik, or wherever. That's my general position.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this page please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit this page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6655, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, in your statement to the Defence, in paragraph 2, you mentioned in the last sentence that you were never -- that you were not a member of the new parties because you did -- because you did not agree with the nationalist platforms of these parties. Mr. Rasevic, it was when these nationalist parties were established that conflicts and ethnic strife started; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I won't call them nationalist parties. They were ethnic parties. Whether they later became nationalist that's for somebody else to assess. But I wasn't there. I'm still a -- I still feel a kind of nostalgia for Yugoslavia, and I don't think that will change ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You yourself stated that you did not agree with the nationalist platforms. That's why I asked you. Anyway, Mr. Rasevic, before the outbreak of the conflict, Dr. Mandic, a medical doctor, one of the SDS leaders in Foca, approached you and wanted you to side with the Serbs and help them to get hold of the armoury arsenal of the KP Dom; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where you got that information. There was a conversation, and I happened to be at the hospital. He didn't say that the weapons should be given to the Serbs. Maybe I made a mistake. He said, Don't let the Muslims get hold of these weapons. And I was against both the Serbs and the Muslims getting hold of those weapons. We were probably the only ones in Bosnia-Herzegovina who destroyed their weapons. That's what we did at the KP Dom. Everybody was arming themselves, but we destroyed over 60.000 pieces of ammunition to prevent both the Serbs and the Muslims to get hold of them. We didn't differentiate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, you testified in your Defence case on the 11th of December, 2007, before the State Court in Bosnia and we will now look at one page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25866 on the screen. And page 9, please, in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S. In the English it's at the end of the page, and in the B/C/S it's on -- on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I quote: "One man saw me there. That man at that time was one of the Serb leaders, and he was -- he has seen -- he was seen as a leader -- a Serb leader during the Focatrans affair as well." And a few lines down: "He asked me, Are you going take your side? And I was thinking, Take what side, in what sentence? And he told me, You cannot be on neither side. What do you think you are going to do with the armoury arsenal or with the armoury storage place?" Next page in the English, please, the B/C/S remains: "And I told him, I'm doing my job. There is no need for me take any sides. And what are you saying about the armoury arsenal, the weapons storage? And he told me, All you have to do is to appoint the guards as we tell you and we'll barge in and take over the armoury arsenal." But then you said: "And I left and went to see the warden and told him about this." Mr. Rasevic, that is what you said then, and that's correct what you said then; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I would repeat the same even now. Nobody could exert influence on me that would have a bearing on the manner how I went about my work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this Serb leader was Dr. Mandic, whom you know as a doctor from the Foca hospital; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, this is the first time I hear that he was a sort of leader in the SDS. I really didn't know that he was a person of importance in their ranks. I can kind of doubt that, really, but I really don't know. I cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then we need to have, again, the -- we have to move to page 14 in the English and page 14 in the B/C/S. It's both in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And your Defence counsel, Mr. Prodanovic asked you: "Before I put your next question, when you talk about the SDS leader who was trying to exert influence on you, can you tell us his name?" And your answer is: It's Dr. Mandic. He worked in the hospital." That's what you said then. You speak, and you did so before, speak of the Serb leader; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That question was phrased by the lawyer. And I replied that it was Dr. Mandic whom I ran into at the hospital. It wasn't because I knew him and went there to see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can these three pages just discussed please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6656, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And after the clashes started and the KP Dom was hit by a rocket, as it was in the middle between the two sides, together with Mr. Tesovic you transferred about 96 non-Serb convicts via Montenegro to the Tuzla prison so that they would be safe, right, that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was our assessment that if we save those people, and they were all ethnic Muslims, Croats, and Albanians, 98 of them, and we did that in agreement with the BH authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on your way, you stopped at the Velecevo female prison and you stayed there for a while; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the first three or four days of the war, I was with the convicts from Foca KP Dom. There was also Alija Berber, the deputy warden, and some 40-odd guards of different ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I'm just talking now about what -- some events in Velecevo female prison and we don't need any more details. My question was only that you stayed there and it's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And at that time you say you saw military men with rank insignia at the Velecevo female prison. It was sort of a command post; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I think that at that time it wasn't a command post, because there were still female convicts in that prison. We arrived there with a total of 125 convicts. Suddenly, on the following day, some soldiers turned up, but I didn't know who they were or what they were. They seemed very aggressive.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on that occasion, while you were in Velecevo you encountered one of your Muslim colleagues from the KP Dom who told you that he was captured and that you and Mr. Tesovic tried to get him released. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. He was a colleague from work, a dentist. We were able to convince those people to let them go and they did. But later on, he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "those people," you convinced those people, that includes Mr. Velibor Ostojic, who was also at Velecevo at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We also spoke to him. He immediately tried to -- but he had problems persuading the soldiers. They were from outside somewhere. I know that he had a hard time persuading them. My impression was that he didn't have the power to take that decision himself. The beginning of the war was a very difficult time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because of your activities to help the non-Serbs convicts out and not siding with Dr. Mandic and the like, Mr. Radojica Tesovic, the warden, was replaced by Mr. Krnojelac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in mid-May, I returned from Serbia where I handed over the prisoners, I went back to my work at the KP Dom, and I learned that Milorad Krnojelac was appointed warden. He said that it was a Crisis Staff that appointed him. Only later, some eight months or so later, the minister of justice confirmed that appointment because, until that time, we had no contact with them, the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you yourself, when returning, experienced harassment and threats and you felt unsafe in your position in the KP Dom; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know how it goes. I felt threats, verbal taunting, why I had protected those convicts of a different ethnicity and taken them to Tuzla. They would surely fight us as soon as tomorrow. But those were only verbal threats. They never became physical. And they were issued by individuals. There were individuals who had already lost someone in the war. And then they would say, You treat them so well and I lost two or three family members, and the like. But nobody from the local authorities ever summoned me to tell me anything that could be described as a threat. Those were all individual problems, and you know, at the beginning, it was difficult to control some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25867.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have, again, the statement you gave to the ICTY, page 184. And you say here: "There was an anathema around me. I was in their black box. I was something like a small Serb or a Serb with a small s. And all I did I did secretly on the sly from my own guards." Mr. Rasevic, you feared your own guards as you did not -- as you did not know who was siding with the SDS policies; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. You know what? People change very quickly in war time. But that did not keep me from doing my job professionally and to show, by way of an example, how this should be done. Some of these guards tried to behave a bit more radically, and in this way I tried to show them that they shouldn't behave that way, and therefore the situation became better and better in terms of the work carried out by the guards, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this page be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add this page to the Exhibit P6655.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, the Krnojelac Trial Chamber in its judgement of 15 March 2002 and I refer here to paragraph 118 on -- on page 50 -- 54 in both pages [sic]. This Trial Chamber found that the non-Serb males from Foca were imprisoned indiscriminately in the KP Dom with no consideration of age, state of health, or civilian status, and that there were many elderly persons among the detained and there was a substantial group of ill, wounded, physically handicapped, and mentally disturbed persons among the detained men; that's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I would not fully agree with that. I can explain why I don't think that is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. There were many elderly persons among the detained, were there not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether there were that many elderly people over the age of 65. I did not have any documents in terms of how old or how young people were. But it is certain that there were no detainees younger than 18 at the KP Dom. Whether there were people of 65 and above, I don't think so. I didn't have that impression. I don't know whether that was the case in the beginning, until mid-May; but after that, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you knew quite number of the non-Serb detainees. Your doctors, your own teacher, your own professor, and even your own colleagues, and you knew that they were civilians and they were not captured during fighting on front lines; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you straight away: It is not for us to assess whether somebody is a civilian or not, that's not within our job description, and whether somebody had been detained rightly or wrongly. Any person in the -- who was brought to the KP -- no person who was brought to the KP Dom, regardless of ethnic background, did not come there without any documents. Then these documents that --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, that's in your statement that was admitted in writing. You do not need to repeat this. I just asking you as a person who knew -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether they had done anything. Those who brought them in knew that. I really don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you repeated the sentence, please, the last bit. The interpreters couldn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had do anything, whether they had committed a crime. That is what those who detained them knew, or rather, they were supposed to know. Now my subjective opinion is something quite different. I had that before the war vis-a-vis certain convicts as well, but that does not change the status.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, in documentation by the Crisis Staff, or later the military command, there was this standard terminology that or that person was captured in war operations, but you knew it's not correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see how I could have known. How could I know? When there is war in town and around, how could I know whether that was or was not the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25866 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it's again your testimony in Bosnia, page 32 in the middle, and then going into 33 in the English. And in the B/C/S, it's 30, the lower part going into page 31. You discuss here with your Defence counsel a certificate of the Crisis Staff of the Serb municipality Foca for Hasan Pilav captured by Serb units. And it's a document from the 26th of April, 1992. Captured in war operations, and so on and so forth. And then asked, you say: "Yes, I knew Hasan Pilav and his wife. "So" -- And your Defence counsel asked you: "So was he captured in combat operations?" And you say, "No." So this is only a form which says war operations, yes, but Hasan Pilav, this specific person was not captured in the combat activities. And your Defence counsel asked you: "So this is only a standard form which would be used to everyone." And your answer is: "Yes." Mr. Rasevic, you knew that it was a pretext for at least the persons you knew -- of whom you knew they were not captured in combat; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, this document has to do with the 26th of April, 1992, when I was in Serbia. I knew Hasan Pilav and his wife. The lawyer was showing a document of the Crisis Staff, and he said, as he defended me, that we, from the KP Dom, were not the ones who made decisions. This is a document from April, and I came from Serbia to the KP Dom only in mid-May. It was the army or the Crisis Staff that issued the document, and nobody could enter the KP Dom or leave the KP Dom without such a document. That was the essence of the question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The end of the sentence, can you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: That was just an introduction. That was evidence provided by us, how somebody was brought to the KP Dom and how people were taken out of the KP Dom. It was certainly not we who were authorised in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this page please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add this to Exhibit P6656.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we have another page of that same testimony. Page 44 in the English, in the middle, and page 41, bottom, in the B/C/S and going over into page 42.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is another document that you discussed in your testimony in Bosnia, and you basically read it out. And it is a telegram by the command of the Herzegovina Corps, dated 14th of January, 1993, with a note of urgent sent to the Command of the Tactical Group Foca, pursuant to the decision of the command of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, the following persons should be released from the KP Dom; namely, Nazif Cengic, Hilmo Cengic, and Fehim Cengic. On 15th January, 1992, they should be transferred. They will be transported the border of Yugoslavia and released. The command shall be informed about after the execution of this order. And signed by General-Major Radovan Grubac. Mr. Rasevic, these Cengics were very old persons; right? They were far beyond 70; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I -- well, they were not old, not all of them. One person was elderly and one person was very young. And I don't see what -- I mean, this is just proof that it was the military command that decided who would be detained and who would be released. And that is what I still assert in general terms. That's how it functioned. There was no other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this exchange was decided by the very top level of the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give any comment on that. I mean, the document is self-explanatory, as far as I can see here, the command of the Herzegovina Corps. I don't see what the top leadership of the RS has to do with this. Whether they decided on that, that is not something that I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can this -- sorry. Can this page please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add that page. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I missed something, but I did not notice an exchange there. It seems to be a unilateral release. Could that please be explained to me? Who was exchanged for who or what? If somebody could explain --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think he could clarify this basically in -- in the examination -- in the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we take a break, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I also have to foreshadow that -- as I already mentioned -- as we already mentioned in the -- in the -- in filing from Friday, for -- the time for cross-examination, the statement has been added to substantially, so I may need perhaps a bit longer but I will only address it when it really arises. Just to foreshadow that this may be coming at some point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We thought one and a half hours would be sufficient, but we'll see how it evolves. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at three past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, the Chamber has looked at the revision of the statement again, and the Chamber is of the view that an additional half an hour would do. Would that be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please have 65 ter 25880 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is a -- a cable of Colonel Marko Kovac of the 31st of August, 1992, to the Trebinje Information Centre. The Foca Tactical group was part of the VRS Herzegovina Corps headquartered in Trebinje; right? That's the chain of command, Mr. Rasevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not very knowledgeable as far as military matters are concerned, but I cannot know what this means. I think it belonged to the Herzegovina corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we have the second page in the -- in the English -- in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if we look at point 5 of this cable, there was a reference that in course of the 30th of August 1992: "We released from prison a total of 55 elderly, unfit Muslim males. "And on 31st August, we released 30 [sic] women and children to keep a visiting commission from discovering them and as an alibi." Mr. Rasevic, this 55 elderly unfit Muslim males, that relates to KP Dom non-Serb detainees; right? That's a transport to Montenegro, you remember?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember these 55. As for the 40 women and children, they were never at the KP Dom. I claim that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: They were in the partisan sports hall; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this release, was it related to the ICRC visit that was basically coming to the KP Dom; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know about that because nobody was duty-bound to inform me. It probably had to do with something, but I don't know what it had to do with. I cannot comment upon things that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In paragraph 35 of your statement, you state that no prisoner was ever killed in the KP Dom. Mr. Rasevic, your regular working hours were until the -- 1500 in the afternoon. That's at least what you say in paragraph 25; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You were not present during night-time with a few exceptions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When there was a regular check of whether the guards were vigilant.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, you cannot honestly claim that no prisoner was ever killed in KP Dom. The best you can claim is that nobody was killed in your presence; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I can claim with a great deal of responsibility that on the premises of the KP Dom, as far as I know, nobody was ever killed. Outside the KP Dom, I cannot say. I don't know. But in the KP Dom, that somebody was killed there, I never heard of any such thing. Even during my trial in Sarajevo, that had not been established.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Krnojelac Trial Chamber established in this regard - and I refer here to 65 ter 25868, pages 132 to 138 in the English, and 120 to 124 in the B/C/S - and I just summarise a few things. Paragraph 33, they find that in the month of June and July 1992, KP Dom guards went to the rooms of the detainees after the roll-call and called out from a list the names of individuals to accompany them for integrations. The persons called out were taken from their rooms to the metal gate at the entrance of the administration building. One by one or in small groups, they were called into the ground floor room of that building. They were taken into one of the rooms, left and right side of the staircase. They were often beaten. The beating lasted well into the evening and sounds of beatings and screams of victims could be heard by other detainees. And in paragraph 334, they refer to when the beating stopped. Victims were sometimes taken to an isolation cell. In other instances, sounds of pistol shots were heard and then the sound of a vehicle with a faulty pipe was heard starting in front of the KP Dom. It was a Zastava KD belonging to the pool of the KP Dom and the reflection of the headlights of the vehicle could be seen by witnesses travelling along the Drina ridge. Mr. Rasevic, do you deny the truth of that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, when a guard receives a list of persons that are to be interrogated by a person, he was only able to take these persons out of the room and to hand them over to the interrogators. That was the only role of the guard. The guard would then return back to his workplace. I claim with full responsibility that in the KP Dom, at least to the best of my acknowledge, and I'm sure that I would have found out in some way -- I'm saying that nobody was ever killed on the premises of the KP Dom. Now whether there was mistreatment during the interviews, during the interrogation by investigator, members of the military, that I cannot say. But on the basis of the knowledge that I have to this day, there were no killings committed in the KP Dom. As for outside the KP Dom, that is something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, the Trial Chamber in your own trial, in Bosnia - and I'll refer here to 65 ter 25871, page 9 -- page 9 and page 2 and 3 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S - they found the very same pattern of events of killing. Do you claim that the witnesses in both these trials did not tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you I tried to slow that down. Unfortunately, I did not management but I'm telling you how it functioned, and I'm telling you what my knowledge was. Witnesses could not really see all of that ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 17, the witness says -- it says here "slow down" and the word is actually "challenge" or "deny." Because, in Serbian, they are very similar: "Usperim,"[phoen] "osperim."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, in your interview with the investigators to the ICTY, you yourself stated that the witnesses told the truth, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as my attitude to them was concerned. I've already stated they testified very correctly. Finally, out of the 38 witnesses of the prosecution of the BH, 36 spoke very favourably about me, but as for certain things, I think that they exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25868 on the screen. That's in English. And the B/C/S is pages 124 to 126. And so 138 in the English; and 124 in the B/C/S. It's actually paragraph 1 -- paragraph 339. 339 -- that's in English it should be on page 138. 138. But it's paragraph 339 on page 138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 120. Oh, no, it's in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In B/C/S it's basically starting. In B/C/S we have the first -- in the very bottom. But the English is ... but I can -- actually it would be easier for the interpreters, though, but I can read the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be coming very soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 137. E-court page 137. E-court page 137 in English. Why do we move the B/C/S, which was correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I can actually read the names. It's about the names. This Trial Chamber -- the Krnojelac Trial Chamber established the -- the -- that 25 victims were killed in the manner that I just described. And in the -- in your own trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the paragraph number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The next page, 138.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It starts -- and now we have the -- lost the B/C/S. Yeah, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You see under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: B/C/S, you see first the name, Alija Altoka, and then on the next page in the B/C/S you see more names, and all together it's also more names on the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, these names should be very familiar to you because in your own trial, in Bosnia, the trial chamber actually came up with the very same names. And I would only want to address one more, and that's the person number -- it was mentioned number 25, and that is Kemal Tulek. Kemal Tulek was your former guard; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you notice that after one such night he was gone, he disappeared?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to work in the morning, they told me that members of the military security took Kemal Tulek away - because all the guards knew him, that's why they told me - that he was taken out for integration, he and I think two or three other persons. So they took him out of the KP Dom. The papers were all properly signed. What happened to him later, I don't know. I think that he is on this list of missing persons or something like that. But that night he was not interrogated at the KP Dom. He was taken away before 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You were not there on that day; right? So you cannot really claim that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I can just claim that he was not killed at the KP Dom. I can claim that because the guards and the duty officer told me that, that he and two or three other prisoners were taken out of the KP Dom. Now whether somebody abused that later, I cannot say because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, in paragraph 30 of your statement, you claim that the detainees did not have a view outside the KP Dom because the administration building obstructed the view. Mr. Rasevic, the building in which the detainees were kept were -- had more floors than the administration building and, thus, the detainees in the top rooms could look over the administration building and see part of the iron bridge over the Drina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They could just see the top of the bridge, the iron bridge, not the bottom. And they could see a house on the opposite bank of the Drina that was a little taller. They couldn't see the road or the actual bottom part of the bridge, lower part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25946 on the screen. And that is a sketch of the KP Dom. And ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, there is your signature on top of this next to the 24th of September, 2004; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the -- certain markings on there are made by you. And my only question is: The room 11, you have indicated room 11 on the building A with windows onto the building B and also windows facing the administration building; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this sketch be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is building 11?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Room 11. There is a marker -- a little arrow next to the tree. The little tree next to building A, you see number 11. Yes. That's where it is. And that indicates room 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Rasevic, room 11 had four -- four separate rooms and also a little main hall and those kind of things; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a collective, as we called it. It had four sleeping areas, washing area, toilet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6657, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now please have Exhibit P03353 on the screen. And this is a set of photos. And we only need to look at the fifth photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, Mr. Rasevic, you recall that a team of investigators visited the KP Dom in summer 1996, and you were among those KP Dom staff members showing them around, and they made photos; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was with them in 1996, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And where this little arrow, yellow arrow is, that's the start of the iron bridge over the Drina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: That is the top part of the iron construction. You cannot see the actual road. You can only see a small section of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this photo would be the view of the detainees, that the detainees had from the top floor of the building where they were housed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I remember when the investigators were there, military prisoners of war were never placed in this small room from where the photograph was taken. It was a few of them. And they were separate from the rest of the inmates. And this is also something that I told the investigators at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In paragraph 30 of your statement, you claim it was physically absolutely impossible for the detainees to see the rooms where interrogations took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have P3569, page 4, on the screen. Page 4. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, the little -- the -- the circle with number 2 indicates where room 11 was; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The investigators measured the distance between the building and the administration building, and they measured it as being 10.2 metres and 11. -- up to 11.75 metres. Would you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I never measured it; but, yes, I believe that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And here these yellow arrows also show where room 11 was, facing the admin building; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the picture below, there is the infamous metal door that all the witnesses spoke about; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: They're not infamous. It's the main entrance to the KP Dom. I don't know why they would be termed as "infamous." This is the only way to come in and out of the facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now please have 65 ter 11289C on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, if you look at the lower photo, that is what the investigators found was the view of the detainees from room 11 had on part of the administration building in which, according to their testimony, night-time interrogations took place. Agree?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where they were interrogated. Night interrogations were forbidden at the insistence of the military authorities at the end of May or June because inmates could not be taken out and guards would not enter the premises of the prisoners and inmates after 2000 hours. This is what was set down in the rules --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the last sentence, please. Interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you understood me. Already by the end of the June, at the insistence of the KP Dom administration, there was request to the army to stop interrogating persons after 2000 hours in the premises of the KP Dom, nor could they be taken out of the KP Dom because this was something that was regulated by our internal rules. I believe that these were premises that were used for interrogations, among other premises that were used for the same purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, could that be a mistake that you said June? Could it be July, end of July? Even August?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't early August. Definitely. Possibly it could have been early July or mid-July. I cannot really remember that anymore. It's been a long time since -- after all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if we look at the next page, that's basically -- it's basically the same -- it's the same window, same room, same view, but there is -- actually some panes were put there to reflect the situation at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since glass was broken because of shooting, we had to improvise something. We didn't have any glass to replace the panes. So this is the sort of protection that was put up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this exhibit please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit P6658.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, you are aware that many of the non-Serb detainees disappeared in so-called exchanges; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that after the war, unfortunately. At the time when people were being taken away, I thought all of that was regular. And I thought that there was permission given for them to be taken out of the KP Dom and that's how it was done. In some cases, that was pursuant to permission, but, in other cases, unfortunately, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the -- the Krnojelac Trial Chamber, and I refer here to page -- paragraphs 479, 4 -- and 480, this -- this -- that Trial Chamber found that in nine such exchanges, between August 1992 to March 1993, between 181 to 223 detainees were taken from the KP Dom and disappeared. That is basically consistent what your -- the trial chamber in Bosnia-Herzegovina also found, that approximately 200 people disappeared; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't determine the exact number, but that a large number of people were taken out under the pretext of exchanges or being released, that is true. Some people were also exchanged, but all of this is in the records that were maintained by the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In paragraph 20 of your statement, you describe the food situation in the KP Dom and you state that: "We never made a distinction between the prisoners of war and the convicts, so the food was cooked in the same cauldron for everyone."
