And today you gave even more details to this effect. Let me put to you what the Krnojelac Trial Chamber found in relation to this. And that's paragraph 442, and they say: "While the Trial Chamber is satisfied that there were certain restrictions on the quantity and the quality of the food available during the conflict, it finds that the food available was not distributed equally among the detainees. Serbs received more food and of better quality than that given to the non-Serbs. Serbs were allowed second helpings at meals and weight loss was negligible during the period of their detention..." And that -- Mr. Rasevic, that was the situation, at least in the year 1992 and until the -- the ICRC came in 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the situation in 1992 was bad for all convicts, as far as food was concerned, and technically it was impossible. Food was cooked in one cauldron. The cauldron was not divided inside into Serb and Muslim sections. The food was the same for everyone. I state that with full responsibility. We did not differentiate when we were distributing food. Everybody had the possibility of receiving visits and having extra food brought in, cigarettes, and so on. This is something that happened. But as for prisoners of war, military prisoners of war, there was nobody who would be able to do that for them. But as for the cauldron, until we fixed the boiler and had enough steam, all the food was cooked in one cauldron that was sent by the army. And finally, one of the men who was distributing food was a Muslim. He was also there distributing food with some other Serbs. I don't know if somebody perhaps received more or less in a portion. I mean, there was always something like that going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, you yourself tried to help and asked the warden to have the leftovers provided to the non-Serb detainees, the leftovers from the Serbs; right? Because they ate later after the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: No, not quite. That depended on the daily schedule set by the warden. He would set the times when food would be distributed. I did ask that food be distributed, extra food, that some of it would be set aside for Serbs who would be eating later and that the surplus would be distributed to the military prisoners of war. I did get permission for this and this was actually done. As for whether this was enough or not, I really cannot say. I think it probably wasn't. I mean, it would be nonsense to say that it was good quality food, but it was food, and it was the only thing that was possible at the time, in terms of quantity and quality.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, in paragraph 25 of your statement, you claim that you have never been present while any of the detainees were beaten or mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never present in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me refer you to an incident that involved the detainee Salko Mandzo, nicknamed Kelta. He was beaten by a dozen military policemen and cut with a knife during the interrogation because they thought he would be a person close to one of the Muslim leaders Saja; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I just happened to be passing by on my way back from the farm, and I could see that they were interrogating somebody. I asked the duty officer. They said they were interrogating Kelta and I kind of stopped and I was saying, What are you asking Kelta? And then one of the interrogators said, We're checking whether he has anything to do with Saja. And I said, What Saja? He is just a miserable person. He couldn't get to Saja. And then they stopped beating hum. It's true I went to -- up to him. I greeted him. He was bleeding. I gave him a handkerchief to wipe the blood off. And I took him back to the compound. He is still alive today. They said that, We have to call the boss. It seems that we have the wrong man. It's not the one that we were looking for. So I had the fortune by just coincidental intervention to save a man.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Rasevic, you were also present when Ekrem Sekovic, after a successful -- unsuccessful attempt to escape on the 8th of July, 1993, was brought back to the KP Dom and he was severely beaten by Borilo after his return; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, first let me say that it was "Ekrem Zekovic," not "Sekovic." He escaped from KP Dom and there was a search organised for him, and probably while they were searching for him, I wasn't there. I spoke with Zekovic later. However, he told me that he was beaten, abused by members of the military security. They wanted him to admit who gave him the clothes that he had on when he escaped. I was actually the one who gave him the clothes. He did not want to admit that. He said to me then, They can kill me, but I'm not going to tell on you. He did not ever tell me that any of the guards had beaten him. He told me that he was interrogated for a few days. I did suggest to him that he should admit that and he said, No, I'm not going to do it. Let it be like this. I talked to Zekovic to this day and we sometimes do talk about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Zekovic, while he was in the isolation cell, he continued to be abused, mistreated; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I came after ten days or so from the coast. I went to the seaside and then I went to see him and I spoke with him. And that's all that he told me, that he was beaten. He didn't tell me when or anything like that. And he came out of the solitary confinement cell very quickly after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the food rations for the non-Serb detainees were half for quite some time, also as a collective punishment; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Really, I don't know whether this was done. I cannot comment on that because I was away for those ten days. I don't know if there was any punishment undertaken during that ten-day period, and if it was, then that was really not all right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can I ask for an explanation? Does the Prosecutor believe -- does the -- is the Prosecution thinking about those ten days, in particular, or in a general period?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was actually only referring to the events surrounding Mr. Zekovic, and that's described also in paragraph 233 of the Krnojelac judgement. But we have no time to go into more details to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, there is one additional point that I would like to discuss with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, do I have enough time? It will take another, let's say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think your time will be up around -- at the end of this session. You have about 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh. That's good to know. That's good to know, because I was running through my script. Then I can actually discuss something else with you, of which I was afraid I had no time. Can we please have 65 ter 25927 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is another document from Commander Kovac from the 20 -- 27th of October, 1993. The -- the date is a little bit difficult to see from -- from this -- in the B/C/S version, but the stamp on the next page, the stamp from the office -- the other office, then you can see it's the 27th. Here, we have this document listing 55 persons, and if you look at the first paragraphs, Mr. Kovac refers to these captured persons as Turks. Turks. Captured Turks. That was the term that the military would sometimes use - right? - "captured Turks"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I think that this would be something that would happen rarely with military officers. I don't see why this term would be used, "Turtci," [phoen] "Turks." I don't see why they would use such a term.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When we look at the list of people, Mr. Rasevic, we see from the year of birth of quite some of them that they are already 50 years of age - correct? - when you look at those born in 1940, 1941. It's quite a number of elderly people here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we briefly move into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 19, that is the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if we look at number 19, that's -- Salko Mandzo listed here, is that the one that you saved from being beaten further?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this please -- can this exhibit please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives exhibit P6659, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you go back to private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, this list of detainees from October 1993 contains only 51 names but, at that time, there were more non-Serbs detained in the KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know why that information was requested for an exchange or release or whatever, but, yes, there were more. The Red Cross had been there before and registered them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, there are only 51 listed here in this list because quite a number of detainees were hidden from the Red Cross so that they were not registered as KP Dom detainees; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if they were hidden. But people would be at work when the Red Cross came to visit because they only gave us half an hour's notice. So I'm not sure how the army handled that. But it is certain that there were more prisoners. And I believe that eventually they were all exchanged.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 24, the witness said, "I don't know that they were hidden." And it was interpreted as, [In English] "I don't know if they were hidden." Not if they had been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see much difference, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25867, page 229 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that's your statement to the ICTY investigators. And -- 229. And there, I ask: "Now that you mentioned the ICRC, you were involved in hiding detainees from the ICRC, were you not?" And you say: "No. The prisoners were hidden from them, that's true. People would come from the military security prior to the visit, and I think this happened once or twice." Mr. Rasevic, that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I still stand by that. It means that the army came and took people away. Whether they were hiding them or whatever they were doing, I don't know. But we, from the KP Dom, did not do that. We were not involved. Finally, all those people were later again registered and exchanged, but what methods were applied and what exactly they did, I still fail to understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, some were never registered, and those not registered were particularly at risk because they could disappear without leaving any trace in the lists of the ICRC or anywhere; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: You know what I think, but that's my personal opinion and without any firm foundation, that there were some prisoners of war who were interrogated and processed. And there was another group who were never interrogated. They were set aside for exchanges against Serb prisoners from other prisons. And I believe that other group, that was not registered, was there only for that purpose, only for exchange, because allegedly the other side had the same practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And one of those was Dr. Aziz Torlak, a medical doctor. Do you remember him being in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he was not registered because he was always hidden when the ICRC came; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say because the army came with a list and took some people away. He may have been, but I'm -- or, rather, that list was not really available to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Aziz Torlak was taken away in summer 1993 for allegedly the need for a battalion of the VRS and he disappeared and he's dead; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I know that he was taken away. I was told that he was taken away to be exchanged. Unfortunately, during my trial, I found out that the -- the exchange never came about. Why not, what happened? No idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, you say in paragraph 13 of your statement that you started to work in the KP Dom in mid-May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25931 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we have a decision of the Warden Krnojelac of 27 April, 1992, appointing you to this position; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But let me explain. On the 27th, I was in Serbia. I only returned after the 1st of May. I know that for sure. And where did this date come from? I don't know. It was probably due to some administrative reasons, but that doesn't change the essence of my work and my information.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic -- sorry. You mentioned your frequent visits to the isolation cells. When you did that, you saw injured -- injuries on the detainees -- looked up there; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: It was my duty and my task to always visit people in isolation cells, and I did see injured people. And I asked whether the injuries had been inflicted by any of my guards, but the answer was, No, this has nothing to do with your guards. And that was all in terms of conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You asked him only about the guards and they said, No, it were not the guards. But they also told you that it were the military police that beat them up; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that I engaged in such a conversation with them. I would often ask them if they had medical problems. If they said yes, I would refer them to the nurse for him to take subsequent steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25866.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it's your testimony in front of the Court, the State Court in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we need now page 114 in the English, and 107 in the B/C/S -- or 108 in the B/C/S. 114. 114 in the -- in the -- in the English. 114. And, in the B/C/S, it is 108.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you speak here with the prosecutor about the solitary cells and what you saw. And then the prosecutor asks: "Does it mean that sometimes when you were visiting solitary cells and when you were visiting rooms, did you ever see a prisoner with injuries? And you say: "Well, yes, there were some bruises on the prisoners that I would spot ..." "Did you enquire? Did you ask them why? How come that they have those injuries?" And your answer is: "My exclusive question was, Did my guards beat you up? Did they do it to you? And the prisoners would tell me, No, the military police officers and the military security officers did that to me." So that's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Possible. Clearly, somebody must have beaten them. If it wasn't my guards, then it would have been the military police or the military security. That is quite possible. I probably said that, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this page please be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add this to Exhibit P6656.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, when you heard that these interrogators from the military police, military security, when they beat up the non-Serb detainees, you did not do anything about that? Not writing a report or restrict access to them? You didn't do anything?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Let me first tell you. Those people had their own superiors. Secondly, I would report all -- everything that I noticed to my warden. But it wasn't actually in writing. I went to see him and told him. And, after that, he must have intervened with the military command because the military was responsible for the interrogation of those people at the KP Dom, not we. I only insisted that my guards should not do that, and I was greatly successful in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, one of your main duties and the duties of your guards under your command was providing the security for all inmates; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That means, if you get aware of persons from outside beating up the detainees you were providing security for, did you not have to stop that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, please. When a guard hands over the facilities for interrogating prisoners of war to the military, the guard did not have the right to enter subsequently and be present at the interrogation. If we noticed injuries, he would inform the warden -- and the warden, the command. And our responsibility ended there. And if anybody needed medical assistance, they would get it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, I want to go back -- and that would be basically my last point. I want to go back to the judgement of the Krnojelac case, paragraph 339 that we looked at before, where we looked at the 25 names of victims that were killed. As this Trial Chamber found -- and this Trial Chamber also found that guards were involved in this night-time interrogations that left people dead. And the guards listed are Milenko Burilo, Zoran Matovic, Milovan Vukovic, Dragomir Obrenovic, Radovan Vukovic, Slavoko Koroman, Dragan Zelenovic, Vlatko Pljevaljcic and Predrag Stefanovic. None of these guards were of disciplined or reported to or investigated for their conduct; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Please. First of all, some of them are not guards of mine at all, Zelenovic, Koroman, who were -- left for the front immediately after, and so on. They weren't there at all. Secondly, I always asked each prisoner, even when I noticed injuries on their bodies, whether any of my guards had been involved in that, and they would always reply, No. And how, based on what, am I supposed to have found out? If anybody was involved, they are responsible for that themselves, and they should be held liable. Even before the war, convicts sometimes would not report physical violence and it would be learned of only subsequently. Whether it was for fear or for any other reason, I don't know. But they said that my guards had not taken part in that, that my guards had nothing to do with it. And then how could I have launched an investigation? Eventually most of them said that most of my guards were very fair to them. If in any individuals did their own thing behind my back, well, that I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, my last question refers to what you said, again, in your statement to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25867 on the screen. And it's page 197 on the bottom and goes over into 198.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say, speaking about your knowledge: "I was shocked to read -- to read what I read," referring to the statements of the people in the Krnojelac case and in the State Court, "they hid it from me. They must have gone to great lengths to hide it from me because if I had known for a second and I understand that those Muslims, that they didn't tell me anything even if I -- if in response to my direct questions, if when I asked them, if they had any problems if anything was wrong, because they must have been afraid of talking. They must have been afraid of further revenge." So you were fully aware that the detainees would never say anything about the guards because they would fear an immediate violent response; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I thought that some people, some prisoners who were at the KP Dom, could trust me fully, and so they were in a position to tell me. Because we had known each other from before. Let me tell you also that among them there were military prisoners of war who ratted on the military security in order to get some benefits. But probably they were more afraid of each other than of the guards and their revenge. Once -- not once did they tell me that my guards had anything to do that -- do -- do with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour can this page be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes we'll add these pages to Exhibit P6655.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Mr. Rasevic, I'll start with the most recent thing on page 63, lines 13 through 15. It was read out, as you said, and I'm going to read out in English: [In English] "If I had known for a second and I understand that those Muslims, that they didn't tell me anything even if I -- if, in response to my direct question, if, when I asked them, if they had any problems if anything was wrong because they must have been afraid of talking, they must have been afraid of further revenges." [Interpretation] Can you tell us if you knew for a fact that they were hiding something or is it the way you stated it here?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I asked people of whom I expected to tell me the truth, and people who thought -- would trust me. And their answer was always that it wasn't the case, that my guards hadn't participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 50 food was discussed. Did Muslim prisoners of war or convicts -- or, rather, were they forced to eat pork?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: No. The Serbs didn't get any pork either because we didn't have enough of it. We didn't get such -- we weren't getting such supplies. So nobody was forced to do so and I believe that they would have eaten it if there had been any. If you take into consideration the situation with regard to food, nobody would have asked questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were the families of the Serbian detainees at the time; and where were those of the Muslim detainees? Who was in a position to bring food?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I am glad you asked this question. Until mid-June, both Muslims -- Muslim prisoners and the others got regular portions. Until 1500 hours, there were columns standing there, waiting. When the Muslims left Foca there was no one left to bring food, possibly some friends occasionally. On the other hand, the Serbs were still there and they were in a position to -- to supply food. However, the Muslim prisoners got regular visits all the way until maybe late June, until the time when the Muslims left Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Line 11 then, it seems to have been interpreted regular portions, did you have regular portions or regular visits?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: You mean in that last case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until mid-June.

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: Regular visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember when the Red Cross visited the KP Dom for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I think it would have been around May 1993. But don't nail me on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then document 25880 -- 25880, the telegram of Mr. Kovac of August -- the 31st of August, actually, mentions a commission that was announced. Did our domestic authorities, the Ministry of Justice, the government, have any control, or did they inspect your prison?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, all the way until 1993, we were totally isolated, in terms of traffic and everything. So the answer is no, they didn't come. They couldn't. They would have had to travel through Serbia and Montenegro, which a very long journey. At any rate, I never noticed anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: D466 is a cabinet decision dated 9 August 1992 about the establishment of a commission to inspect collection centres and prisoners. Did Mr. Kovac mention the announced visit of the Red Cross in August 1992, according to what you know now, what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I was in no position to communicate with -- if you mean Colonel Kovac. He was the military commander and he mostly communicated with the prison warden. Whether he announced anything to him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Those elements from the military that you have mentioned, were they under full control? Were they fully disciplined? Could one say that they were acting as a disciplined army?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: You know something? When a war begins, one system breaks down and another isn't established yet. And then there are groups who -- that roam about, and for a time, at least a month or so, they were difficult to control. They were coming in from all over the place, Serbia, Montenegro. It was very difficult to cope with them. It was only the army that was in a -- that had the ability to control them. We were preventing several attempts by paramilitary formations to enter the KP Dom. You think it was easy? No, sir. But we were able to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 24866, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report following the inspection of the public security stations of Foca, Cajnice, Rudo, but we're not interested in that. But Foca is on page 1. It says here that the -- they were unable to find the court and the prosecutor's office. The names of the persons were known but they had left.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot find where the accused is reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you -- could you indicate from where you are reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph -- ah, the second-but-last paragraph from the bottom. No, actually, in English, it must be on the following page. In Serbia, it's the last-but-one, starting with the words [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't really understand to which particular part of my cross-examination these police statistics could refer. I did not address these kinds of matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hmm. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please turn back one page in the English. Excellencies, here the witness said that his guards were fair, but that in the army there were some elements that were in a position to act differently. This document shows that such elements disarmed the police, the regular police, and beat them up and maltreated them. This is what I want to show so that we -- so we'll see that the last sentence states that it was ordered to document war crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you. I'll ask you. Can you see this last but one paragraph where it says: "Police was disarmed and mistreated ..." How does that tally with your experience of some elements who were not only mistreating Muslims but also Serbs and even the police?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: My wife also worked at the MUP, so I know about that. I know that they mistreated them. They disarmed all the MUP employees and threw them out, and this went on for several days, I think. And I also said that they tried to attack us at the KP Dom, too, but we somehow managed to fend them off. So these were people who took power into their own hands. Now what was their aim? Looting, all sorts of things. Can you imagine in a town like that where there is no electricity, where we were blocked, we didn't have electricity for two or three months, it was very hard to keep them under any kind of control, and I believe that this is what this report pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that they took power into their own hands. I think that that should be interpreted differently, not this way that it has been interpreted. What was the attitude of the authorities in relation to mistreatment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still think that this has nothing to do whatsoever with the cross-examination. The cross-examination was focussing on the events within the KP Dom and about a pattern of official access to detainees and what happened during interrogation. It had nothing to do with the -- what was happening between the Serbs outside in Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not related to the pattern of military police abusing their powers? I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll allow the accused to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the authorities in relation to these people who took power into their own hands? I don't like that interpretation. I would prefer alienated from the power. So what was the attitude of the authorities towards these things that happened that caused trouble for you as well in terms of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the authorities tried to resolve this problem, and they did manage to do it within a few days with the assistance of the military command and active-duty police officers. So after a few days, the situation returned to normal, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit D4312, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it was your intentional decision not to tender 65 ter 25880, which included facts from Foca?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, actually, I intended to tender all the exhibits that I pulled up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic also dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit that as Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6660, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, shall we continue after a break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, no. I'll finish before -- before the break, Excellency. Only two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, then please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, Mr. Rasevic, was the sports hall a prison?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was some kind of a reception centre from which people were transported to wherever they wanted to go. Muslims, in the direction of Montenegro, they could not go in any other direction, and then further on towards Macedonia, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was also mentioned that you confirmed that one detainee did not take part in the armed rebellion. Did the army only capture those who were caught with a rifle in their hands on the separation line, or were there other crimes committed against the military for which they could arrest people and bring them in?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: You know, not a single military POW could have been brought in without an accompanying document from the military. So that document would say that such a person is being brought into custody because of the commission of a war crime. Where? We don't know. Some people were arrested in combat. Others were arrested in town. Then whether they committed certain incriminations somewhere, we don't know, but that is what the documents would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Last question. You said that in Velecevo there were some soldiers who were not from Foca. What was the army then that was official in Foca and that was officially present in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MITAR RASEVIC
utterances.text: You know that's the beginning of the war. These were self-organised people. They organised themselves until the Army of Republika Srpska was re-established. Now these people who came, my feeling was that they had come somewhere from Serbia. Who they were, I think that even in -- they didn't even belong to an organised army in Foca. Quite simply, they entered. It was a porous border. They were very aggressive. By the way they spoke, I cam to the conclusion that they were not from Foca because they did not speak Ijkavian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rasevic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, what did you mean when you said they didn't speak Ijkavian? Ijkavian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not speak Ijkavian. Let me be clear. They did not speak the language that is spoken in our area, in Bosnia. Ekavian is spoken in Serbia and in parts of Montenegro, so on that basis I concluded that they were not from our region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Rasevic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. You may be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon. You are the first judge who presided over my hearing. Thank you. It's a pleasure to see you. I wish you good health and lots of luck, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and thank you. Just before the break, I just wanted to indicate that with regard to the next witness, and the Rule 90(E) warning, last week we had indicated that he does not need a warning. That was before the additions to the statement. In light of the new topics, I will be going into areas where I think a warning would be appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, it's noted. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.36 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Klickovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, before you commence your evidence, Mr. Klickovic, that -- I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal. That is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to admission of guilt for a criminal offence, or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But, in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Klickovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us please speak slowly. Let us pause between our questions and answers so that it would all be recorded in the transcript. Have you provided my Defence team with a statement?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D9687. Could we please have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the first page of that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please do not be confused by the fact that many paragraphs were taken out of your statement. The reason is the fact that your municipality is not in my indictment so the participants in these proceedings, the Chamber and the Prosecutor, were not interested in that part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could the witness now be shown the last page so that he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Taking this into account, namely, that these paragraphs were taken out of your statement, what remains in your statement, does that faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Everything that remained in the statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom as were those that were put to you when you took -- when you gave this statement, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answers would -- well, perhaps not exactly identical in terms of sequence of words and thoughts, but in form they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement into evidence according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objections, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit D4313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out in the English language a summary of Mr. Gojko Klickovic's statement and then I'm going to put a few more questions. I'm going to deal with that live. [In English] Gojko Klickovic served as the chairman of the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanska Krupa between December 1991. After that, he was appointed it's the president of Crisis Staff of Bosanska Krupa, and when the war broke out, he became president of the War Presidency of the municipality. He served two terms as a prime minister of the Republika Srpska. In December 1997 -- in December 2007, the office of the BH prosecutor charged Mr. Klickovic with participation in a joint criminal enterprise, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. He was later acquitted of all allegations in both first instance and the appeals judgement. Mr. Klickovic was present at the session of the Main Board of the SDS in Sarajevo when the manual was distributed and that became known as the Variant A and B. This manual had no binding character and everything in it was in accordance with the applicable laws. Mr. Gojko Klickovic states that nobody ever advocated the creation of an ethnically pure Serbian state on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In July 1996, as prime minister, he was asked to ensure that President Karadzic complies with the agreement that Karadzic himself had reached with Holbrooke. He was told that President Karadzic had been promised by Holbrooke that he would not be prosecuted in The Hague if he steps down. Dr. Karadzic was a real democratic leader. He did not easily resort to issuing orders as instruments of power, and all his orders and decisions were in keeping with the laws and regulations, states Mr. Klickovic. His main objective was to fight for people, for life, for peace, and stability in every situation. And that is short summary. Now I would like to pose several questions to Mr. Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, I would like to put a few questions to you. As member of the Main Board, not an official in your municipality, could you now tell the Trial Chamber how come this happened? How come you got interested in the SDS and how come you took part in its creation?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: I will say that I was on the Main Board of the SDS from July 1991. Actually, have been until this day. That is to say, that I have been a member of the SDS throughout. So from the very outset, when the party was founded in 1990, I was an active member, because I was attracted by the programme of the Serbian Democratic Party. Its intention was basically to preserve the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and to preserve the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia. How do I put this? For me, that was guarantee that the Serb people would remain in a single state. It was a guarantee for me that peace would be preserved in that way and it was easier to do that in a big powerful Yugoslavia rather than in some small partially states that were already being heralded, because things started getting quite heated from 1989 onwards, and it became obvious that this creation of the West was now being dismantled by the West itself. The programme of the SDS, the way I saw it, was at first the programme of the Serbian Democratic Party from Croatia. That was the programme of the party that was led by Dr. Raskovic, a kind man, a psychologist, a doctor, a humanist. And this programme established the basic principles, and I was attracted by these basic principles because when I first started working, my job was in the -- then League of Communists of Yugoslavia, in the municipal committee of Bosanska Krupa, and this idea that was contained in that political organisation and party, it was quite simply accepted in this new programme of the future Serbian Democratic Party that also just wanted to preserve Yugoslavia and to spare those areas of a new war. Any kind of separation without the consent of others in the former Yugoslavia would have led to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that in 1989 things started getting heated, as you said. What did you mean by that? And did you have any insight in terms of what was going on in Yugoslavia or at least in your own neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as an official in the League of Communists, beforehand, and also as a person who was a scholar, I certainly was familiar with the situation in the former Yugoslavia and especially things became totally clear to me after the 11th Congress, when, in fact, it became obvious that Yugoslavia would be dissolved. The very fact that the League of Communists was separated into different republics and this federalisation meant that Yugoslavia was on the path of conflict and that, as such, Yugoslavia would not stay on because the retrograde forces, particularly in Croatia and Slovenia, not only in 1989 but before that, in 1987 and 1988, they showed their true face. Let me just say something else. If we look at 1987, what happened in May, when the doctrine and strategy of All People's Defence was being adopted, or rather, of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, it became obvious already then that there were states within a state. That is to say, there is Slovenia in Yugoslavia, there is Croatia in Yugoslavia, and also Macedonia was sort of inclined towards that too. It already became obvious that the west and different services were working on the breakup of Yugoslavia. Not to speak about resistance vis-a-vis the state institutions of Yugoslavia. That meant the defence of the area, especially the secretariat of the interior and the army. So that is where it first became evident that Yugoslavia would be broken up. As for these individual phenomenon, we can speak about this at great length. Already in 1988 and 1990 there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us briefly about the organisational and election activity of the SDS in your region, what its intonation was and how you would assess it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that that region or, rather, this area of the then-Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina approached election activities in a rather tolerant manner on the eve of the first multi-party elections in this area, probably because of the agreements that had been reached at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, between the HDZ, the SDA, and later on, the SDS too. I'm saying "later the SDS" because the SDS was the last one to be organised as such, and you yourself witnessed the fact that Alija Izetbegovic already in July 1990 warned the Serbs, saying, What are you waiting for? Why don't you get organised too. It is time for us to move onto democracy, a multi-party system, and so on. As for this area, there was good co-operation in this period between the SDA -- actually, Muslims were the majority population in our area, but there were also Croats and the HDZ and also another party, the SDP, the Socialist Alliance, and so on. So there were others, but the key forces were the Party for Democratic Action and the Serb Democratic Party that were rather fair-minded, and they also attended each other's rallies. Perhaps I could even say that they helped each other organise their respective infrastructures because both parties wanted to prepare these first multi-party elections in the best possible way so that these forces of Communism, or rather, socialism could be overcome. All of that was rather -- pretty good, if I can put it that way. The relations were based on tolerance and understanding. I think that it was the month of October 1991 when at this rally in Velika Kladusa, there was that mass gathering and that showed that, after all, the SDA would work together with the HDZ and other Croat parties that had already been organised, not only in Croatia but also in the area of Herceg-Bosna, in our areas where there was a Croat population, because they tied together the two flags, and they said that they would move together towards victory. That is to say, that in the future government, in the future parliament, in the future institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they would function together and that they would try through outvoting to resolve all problems. All right. I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that you gave an answer to my next question - what the basis for the coalition was - but I see that basically you have answered that question. When did tensions arise? When was there a deterioration in relations when the new government started functioning, the one that replaced the regime and the system as such?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Already in 1991; that is to say, as soon as this joint government was established together, these joint authorities and we all participated in that, on the basis of the outcome of the election. Already during the first four months, there were some disagreements. Parties that had a full majority and that were dominant in the executive and in parliament, they wanted to establish in the administration as well the same kind of relations. If one looks at the population in these areas, I will give a specific answer. Bihac, Bosanska Krupa, and other municipalities in the surrounding area, they had a minority. They participated in all of this with less than one-third, that is to say, that the other side could outvote them, and they could do whatever they wanted to do. The first such misunderstanding happened when there was a rationalisation of the staff in these structures. It was supposed to be brought in line with the population structure, which meant that a lot of Serb employees would be dismissed. Of course, this led to tensions and also problems in the assembly and the Executive Board and other organs of government. This was certainly how other problems surfaced too. The next problem that appeared and that was present all the time was the attitude towards the institution of the Yugoslav People's Army. We know that in 1991 there was this resolution, or perhaps we can say it was a declaration. The Assembly of the Serb people made it known that Serbs would respond to JNA call-up. That is to say, they would serve in the armed forces because Yugoslavia officially existed all the way up until midnight on the 25th of April when the new "zabljak" constitution was adopted and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established on that basis. We thought, as legalists, that for as long as Yugoslavia existed and for as long as there were regulations in force that we had to abide by these regulations. And certainly, as for the institution of the armed forces, we saw that institution as a protection and safety for the Serb people because we knew that the Serb people were living in different places that were not interconnected, all the way from Slovenia to Macedonia. So we struggled for the survival of these federal institutions, and we wanted to give our full contribution to the work of these institutions. The Serbs served in the JNA. They were deployed in the structure of the armed forces, and they regularly responded to call-up. This kind of response meant being dismissed from work, being jobless, and it led to problems and torture in that area. Once they would return from the reserve force and from the territories of Croatia where we were deployed to serve in the armed forces of Yugoslavia, there were unpleasant things that happened in the area of Bihac, Krupac, Petrovac, Sanski Most, Novi Grad because these people were being singled out, labelled, threatened, from different sides. They were being told that they should not respond to the call-up, that they should not serve in the JNA. As opposed to others, we did that, and this was this other conflict that clearly showed that it would not be possible to continue that way for a long time with this kind of structure of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us -- actually, you said that young Serbs served in the military. Where were young men, Muslims and Croats, from your area, and did you have any information about their military organisation and arming?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Since the municipality of Bosanska Krupa and, later on, the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa is along the border with Croatia, we knew full well what was going on in the surrounding area, and we were aware of everything that was going on in that area. We responded to this call-up. Others did not. We went to serve in the forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the legal force, but the other members of the armed force - I'm referring to Bosniaks, rather, Muslims at the time - they, within their territorial units and units in local communes, compiled lists, conducted training, decided who their commanders would be along party lines and on the basis of party discipline. That is to say, that they ask not respond. They didn't want to talk about going into the armed force that they were a member of because they all had military cards of the former Yugoslav People's Army. They were all deployed in various units. They had their own assignments; but, according to the orders issued by the party, the SDA, they stayed at home. They -- they went over weekends to conduct exercises organised by the Patriotic League, the Green Berets, and so on. But, at any rate, these were units of at the time that could not fit into any law or legal provision that had to do with All People's Defence in Yugoslavia. That is to say, that these were units that acted outside the system but under the auspices of powerful political parties because the SDA was certainly the most powerful political party in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So these were these first problems, and that was when there was a hint of the problems that were yet to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now go back to domestic politics now. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, in view of your long mandate at the top of the Serbian Democratic Party, who and how was the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party set and what was the role of the Assembly, the Main Board, the Executive Board and the president in the party during the time that you were in the leadership?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say the real truth and the essence regarding the way we worked because I was a member of the Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was a member of the Main Board. For a while, I was in the Executive Board, and also, for a while, I was the director of the directorate of the Serbian Democratic Party so that I can say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you speak very slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat what you said after saying: "I was a member of the Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party," and then everything else. Slowly.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was a member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. I was, for a brief period, a member of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. For a while, I was the director of the directorate of the Serbian Democratic Party. Now I am still a member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. So I really am in a position to reply to this question definitively as to how and in what manner it worked and functioned from the top, all the way down: From the Assembly, down to the SDS Local Board. In essence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now, can you tell us what the role of the Assembly was? Who set policy, who changed the policy, who implemented the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: I was just about to say that the democratic principle was the basis on which the programme goals were established, as well as the main tasks of the Serbian Democratic Party. Everything that was adopted was done exclusively and only in the Assembly, by the Assembly, which was convened once a year, and, if there was any need, it could be convened twice or even more often. However, in practice, it was convened once a year. This would be when the report would be submitted, as well as when the programme would be set for the following year for the Executive Board of the Assembly, for the president. The Main Board, in the meantime, would also convene but rarely, perhaps twice a year, only to analyse what had been done or implemented of the conclusions from the annual assembly session. When the programme was being prepared, or any other conclusion, a broad number of people took part in this process who were not necessarily members of the party. Certain institutions also took part, academic institutions, writers' associations, and they would help to prepare certain programme tasks because the programme of the Serbian Democratic Party was more of a people's programme, a source programme, the goal of which was to maintain or preserve peace in that area, to try to preserve Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and its goal was also to maintain good relations in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was Yugoslavia in -- in -- in a small scale. And it was the only party that propagated idealogical reconciliation in that area. People divided amongst themselves, and this was present among the Serbs and among other nations as well. Serbs had Communist and anarchists, so the idea of the programme was to erase these ideological differences and to establish relations of tolerance, full respect, regardless of anybody's views. The methodology and the way the Serbian Democratic Party operated in these organs was really so tolerant that all the actors, all the participants, could discuss for however long they wanted if they had something new to present. There was no restriction, no obstruction, in this, and I also think that at that time nobody was excluded from the Serbian Democratic Party because they had a different opinion, except for one person who was a bit more radical and who deviated from the party concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us this: You mentioned that you were present when the instructions known as instruction A and B was distributed. Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber on what basis did the Serbian people and the Serbian Democratic Party opt in favour of...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to repeat the last part of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last part question -- your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This procedure of regionalisation, regionalisation, was there any legal or constitutional basis for this process?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that this is a very broad question, and I'm going to attempt to answer just in bullet notes because this is actually a whole set of questions. I would like to be clear and precise, and I don't want to take up too much time when I do this. Let's me start from regionalisation. We know that regionalisation was also set by the Law on the Territorial and Functional Organisation in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the constitution. Some matters were regulated by amendments from 1976, 1989 and 1990. It is correct that only the names or titles were changed, or the headings, depending on the political situation and the circumstances at that particular point in time in a specific area. Here's an example. The Autonomous Region of the Krajina. That was a regional -- or it was an association of the municipalities of the Banja Luka region which rested on the same principles as the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka or the Association of Municipalities of Bihac to which we belonged. In the first stage, it was organised also in keeping with the current laws and the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Other than giving political connotations to these regions, there is nothing of particular importance there. They were dealing with the same questions, the same problems; but, again, I say this depended on the situation and the moment in time in which that particular community was acting. And it is correct that later there was regionalisation along national lines or ethnicity so that we had this regionalisation, which means that the Croats organised the HAO, the Muslims organised MAO, and the Serbs organised SAO, but all of that was the same, with the same goal to resolve some problems faster and in a more organised way, and in case of any kind of danger or endangerment to resolve the security factor more easily. Therefore, this was completely founded in the constitution and the law. As far as the creation of these regional communities is concerned, which later became autonomous regions, and this was something that was valid for Serb, Muslims, Croats, and Bosniaks. That would be a part of the answer. As for the second part, the instructions that really -- this is something that I have to say. This instruction was the basis for action and for the work of the prosecutor's office. Unfortunately, in my own proceedings, I asked the prosecutors 30-odd times why they do not say which law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the law of the defence of the republic or the constitution I violated and why I was brought to the -- before the court. What was it that I did that was counter to the laws that were then in effect? This is a document probably that has been misused and that will be studied for a long time in legal history. Because, in itself, it meanings nothing. As far as I'm concerned, as a member of the Main Board and as an official at the local level, it meant nothing to me. And I did not even take it at the Holiday Inn conference room when it was distributed. I think that it was distributed upon your insistence. You said, Distribute it, for God's sake, and everybody can read it for themselves and then they can see what they want to do then. In itself, the document has no legal force. I didn't even deal with it, but it was just out of party discipline that I looked to see what was actually written there. The instruction that was drafted was drafted, in my opinion, for the purpose of establishing, I would say, a -- a code of behaviour in the field, in complex situations because we already, at that time, in 1991, had a pretty complex situation in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was dictated by an even more complex and worse situation in Croatia. And I believe that the document really did receive a lot of publicity, negative publicity, and it was considered as the bearer of all evil in that area. When you look into it in more detail, the document was formed and is based in the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1974, also based in -- on the Law of All People's Defence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1982, based on the Law on All People's Defence of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1984 and 1987, and also in the strategy and the doctrine of the armed forces which was published on the 25th of May, 1987, in the Law on Yugoslav People's Army from 1985, in the Law on Armed Forces from 1985, in certain provisions of the republican Executive Council of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the election result of the party elections, in the plebiscite of the Serbian people held in 1991, and recommendations of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 11th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask you to be a bit more brief.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to cut it short. Every word from those instructions could be found in some of those 250-odd articles of these laws that I have referred to. I worked on some of those regulations. I know that, and that is why I assert that the document is completely irrelevant in order to establish war crimes. According to the document, there should have been no war crimes at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the interpretation. Are you able to tell us -- you mentioned the recommendations of the 11th of December. Where you thinking of the recommendation on the formation of Serbian municipalities, Serbian municipalities assembly -- municipal assemblies where there were conditions for such a thing?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And these were recommendations from a joint session of the Assembly in which all three peoples took part, and it was stated there that regionalisation should not be used in a negative way, in order to raise interethnic tensions. We needed to wait a little for the joint Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina to adopt the regulations and to regulate this and then the -- the -- the process of regionalisation should proceed. And these recommendations from the 11th of December actually preceded the drafting of these instructions, which somebody later called Variant A and B. It's not a variant. It's just something that depends on the situation where these regulations were supposed to be applied. So these recommendations practically initiated the political organisation of behaviour in the field in order to prevent conflicts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you -- may I just ask you something? I don't have LiveNote if something is not. I am afraid. Are the booths working?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While it is working on the common drive, it does not work on the personal one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right. It's good that it's working somewhere at least. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: When did you adopt this decision in your municipality? Actually, in the question, there are some errors. The question is wrong in lines 6 on page 91; 7, onwards, these are assemblies of the Serbian people in these municipalities. When did you decide in your municipality to form the Assembly of the Serbian People?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: This decision on the formation of Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa was taken in December -- actually -- 1991. It was supposed to have been taken in June 1991. But listening to you, actually, we kept postponing this in the hope that we would repair relations because the discussion on the formation of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, in accordance with the Law on Referendum of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1975 was implemented in the course of the summer, and we prepared -- and we prepared to round off our municipality and inform all the political factors about it from the SDA in the Bosanska Krupa municipality. This would be the SDA at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, up to the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic and yourself, as well as all of our Presidency members. Therefore, we could have done this much earlier, but we expected that at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina a solution would be found so that we would not have to do this in a moment that was full of tensions, that was tense, i.e., not to form the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, which, in the institutional sense, was already completed, but we made it official in December. We formed our organs and set off with working in a normal way without trying to initiate any conflicts with our parts in the SDA. This is about the municipality. We accepted this as some kind of necessary resolution -- solution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you began in June and took the decision in October and completed it in the 11th of December; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Because the dates were not recorded. That is, in June or July, you began; and October you took the decision; and the process ended on the 11th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just a second. Please speak slowly, both of you. Please continue. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's be clear about the dates. The public discussion about the economic justification for the establishment of the municipality had been over by June 1991. We got the mandate to establish the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. In October of the same year, we decided to do that after the continued conflicts within the authorities with the SDA. On the 11th of December, 1991, we officially constituted the Assembly and all of its bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If that was done before the instruction dated 19 December, based on what was it done?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: The instruction of the 19th of December was something that we didn't need at all. Because we had laws and regulations of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were in force, and they provided for -- for the organisation of assemblies according to certain procedure and so on. So we proceeded in accordance with the Law on Referendum and the Law on Territorial Organisation, and we also submitted an application to the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to give us approval. They never did. But they never refused us either. Other municipalities, such as Brod, Modrica, and others were singled out and criticised for such activities. We acted in accordance with laws and regulations in force and that was in line with the programme of the Serbian Democratic Party, which was fully legalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the war broke out, what kind of connections do you have with Pale? And what kind of connections existed between your neighbouring municipalities in Pale? How did you work in your municipalities, you and your colleagues from the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, the Serbian municipality of Bihac, then Bosanski Novi, we had very bad communication because there were problems with the telecom, and it's generally known why, we could only communicate with you at Pale through the delegates and the club of representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party, which you favoured. And you always said that there was no need to -- to double these activities because the delegates and the Assembly were elected representatives of the Serbian people. Therefore, meetings of the Main Board often didn't take place. There would have been a doubling of functions, there would have been costs for travel, and instructions, if required, could be brought by delegates. At any rate, I and my co-workers at the municipality didn't have a great need to consult anyone because we knew the programme of the party, and we knew the laws and regulations, and we adhered to them. The instruction or any other document of imperative character were not binding. We didn't see it as such. There were only there in case anything unforeseen should happen on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what you know about the preservation of peace and legality and law and order, as well as combatting of crimes in your municipality and neighbouring ones, with respect to the participation of the Main Board and the authorities. You may remember who was number one at Mrkonjic Grad or Prnjavor or Laktasi, how the line of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party functioned in these municipalities and others?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember almost each member of the Main Board by municipality, but I can answer generally that the members of the Main Board, where they exerted the most influence in those municipalities the inter-ethnic relations were best. I was a member of the Main Board at Bosanska Krupa; At Novi Grad, it was Mr. Pasic; At Sanski Most, Mr. Brkes; at Petrovac, Mr. Novakovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
utterances.text: At Petrovac, it was Mr. Novakovic; at Gradiska, Mr. Ivastanin; at Srbac, Kupresanin, Milincic, and so on. There were all people who were first-day members of the SDS, and they knew the basic principles upon which the SDS was built. And, in that sense, we weren't faced with many negative things or a negative attitude towards Bosniaks or Croats. Tolerance was present very long. Actually, until the SD --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please start over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, if you could repeat your answer from where you referred to tolerance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was speaking about the members whom I listed. We really paid great attention to tolerance, and we cared about good relations between Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks, and we didn't allow any negative events, because that was also our task in the field that we had got before the conflict. We knew that this was the condition to mitigate the conflict. We expected that Europe, the west, would resolve the problem, and that there would be no conflict. We never expected a war to break out, especially in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I think that wherever we were in positions of responsibility, we, from the SDS, human resources were well protected, and people were able to go to safer places. For example, at Novi Grad, during conflicts, there were also some -- there was also some influence from outside, and JNA units were moving. The Muslim population was offered temporary shelter at Banja Luka or Doboj, but I know from my daily contacts that many left for third countries or other countries that used to be part of former Yugoslavia. At Mrkonjic, we -- there was Luka Culic, a member of the Main Board. They were faced with great problems. They had to protect churches and other buildings from -- even from Serbs who did not agree with them. At Bosanska Krupa, where I was, when there was combat along the Una river where there are mostly Muslim-populated places, we had to act to preserve the lives of those people, and we were successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now very briefly, you mentioned the rifts in the Serbian people, divisions into left and right Serbs. Were the divisions among the Muslims? And were there any entities with which you had good relations?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC
